title: AXA's First-Half Earnings Reach 4.5 Billion Euros, and Its New 2027-2029 Plan Targets 7% to 9% EPS Growth
summary: AXA reported on July 31 that underlying earnings per share rose 8% to 2.19 euros, then used its September 15 investor day to set a new three-year plan with a 75% payout ratio.
description:
AXA, the French insurance group, published its first-half 2026 results on July 31 and followed them on September 15 with a new three-year strategic plan. This article was first published in August and has been updated on October 13, 2026 to correct the release date and add the plan. Taken together, the two announcements show a group that is growing earnings at the top of its target range while deliberately stepping back from parts of the market where prices are falling.

The half-year numbers, from AXA's own press release, were strong. Underlying earnings per share were 2.19 euros, up 8% from the first half of 2025, which the company said was at the top end of its 6% to 8% target range. Underlying earnings were 4.5 billion euros, up 4% reported, or 9% excluding AXA Investment Managers, which AXA sold to BNP Paribas on July 1, 2025. Revenues, defined as gross written premiums and other revenues, rose 5% to 66.3 billion euros. Property and casualty gross written premiums were 35.1 billion euros, up 3%, and life and health premiums were 31.2 billion euros, up 8%.

By business line, property and casualty underlying earnings were 3.2 billion euros, up 6%, with AXA XL earnings up 4%. Life and health underlying earnings were 2.0 billion euros, up 11%. Insurance Business, reporting on the results, put the property and casualty combined ratio at 90.1%, personal lines premiums up 8% to 12 billion euros and commercial lines premiums up 1% to 21.3 billion euros. The combined ratio is the share of premiums paid out in claims and costs, so a figure below 100% indicates an underwriting profit. The group's Solvency II capital ratio, a measure of how well it can absorb losses, was 218% on June 30, up 3 points from January 1, which the release describes as measured after grandfathering. That figure includes a theoretical allowance for dividends and buybacks.

The most striking detail was in reinsurance. According to Insurance Business, AXA XL cut reinsurance premiums by 9% to 1.8 billion euros in the half, with pricing down 5%, after a 7% reduction in the first quarter. The report framed this as a choice of margin over volume rather than a retreat from poor business. It also cited Aon's estimate that global reinsurance capital is at a record 785 billion dollars in 2026, and Guy Carpenter's index showing property catastrophe rates on line down 16% at midyear. AXA XL's Middle East business recorded a loss of 0.1 billion euros, which added 0.4 percentage points to the group loss ratio. In plain terms, insurers who sell cover to other insurers are being paid less for the same risk because there is more capital chasing business, and AXA chose to write less rather than accept lower prices.

The strategic plan, announced on September 15 and titled "Growing Forward," sets out what AXA wants to achieve from 2027 to 2029. The company's targets are 7% to 9% annual growth in underlying earnings per share between 2026 and 2029, an underlying return on equity of 15% to 17%, and about 25 billion euros of cumulative organic cash upstreamed from subsidiaries to the parent over 2027 to 2029. It plans a total payout ratio of 75% of underlying earnings per share, made up of a 60% dividend payout and annual share buybacks equal to 15%, with the dividend per share at least equal to the prior year. AXA said dividends and buybacks would come before any acquisitions.

The plan also gives a guide to 2026. AXA expects underlying earnings of about 8.6 billion euros, EPS growth at the top of the 6% to 8% range and a return on equity at the top of a 14% to 16% range. On capital, it expects to generate 25 to 30 points of Solvency II ratio per year on a normalised basis, and it estimates that a revision of the Solvency II rules expected in the first quarter of 2027 would add about 17 points to the ratio. These are company targets and estimates, not guarantees, and they depend on markets, claims experience and regulation.

On strategy, AXA says it will aim to gain market share in property and casualty for retail, small business and mid-sized companies and in life and health, which together made up 83% of 2025 revenues. AXA XL, at 17% of revenues, will practise what the company calls disciplined cycle management amid softening market conditions. The company also flagged structurally growing areas, namely life and savings, direct distribution and inclusive insurance, and said it would expand life and savings capabilities in its own agencies and with independent advisers and specialist brokers.

Artificial intelligence features in the plan, with AXA targeting annual recurring benefits of 500 to 700 million euros before tax by 2029 across sales, contact centres, pricing, underwriting, claims and support functions. The plan assumes a normalised natural catastrophe load of 4.5 points of the combined ratio and moderating property and casualty pricing, including a softer large commercial market.

What does this mean for customers and investors? For policyholders, falling reinsurance prices tend to feed through to lower prices for commercial property cover over time, though personal lines such as home and motor depend on local claims costs. For investors, the combination of a high payout ratio and a 218% solvency ratio suggests ample capacity to return cash, but the plan relies on growth in life and health to offset a softer property market. For the industry, AXA's willingness to shrink reinsurance rather than chase prices is a signal that discipline, not volume, is the priority at this point in the cycle.

Readers should note that the figures come from company documents and trade press, and that the plan's targets are projections. The next scheduled data point will be the group's later-year results.

key_points: AXA's first-half 2026 underlying earnings were 4.5 billion euros, up 4% (up 9% excluding AXA IM, sold in July 2025), and underlying EPS rose 8% to 2.19 euros.
Revenue rose 5% to 66.3 billion euros; property and casualty earnings were 3.2 billion euros (up 6%) and life and health earnings 2.0 billion euros (up 11%).
The Solvency II ratio stood at 218% on June 30, up 3 points from January 1.
AXA XL's reinsurance premiums fell 9% to 1.8 billion euros as pricing dropped 5%, which Insurance Business reported as a deliberate retreat from softening terms.
On September 15 AXA unveiled its 'Growing Forward' plan: 7% to 9% EPS growth, 15% to 17% ROE, about 25 billion euros of cash upstream and a 75% payout ratio.
why_it_matters: AXA is one of the world's largest insurers, so its results and strategy show where the global insurance cycle is heading. Falling reinsurance prices, strong life and health growth and a heavy emphasis on shareholder returns signal how big insurers plan to behave as property catastrophe pricing softens.

title: Singapore's MAS Consults on a Protected Cell Company Framework to Grow Captives and Insurance-Linked Securities
summary: The July 7 to August 7 consultation would let one legal entity hold segregated cells for captive insurance, cat bonds and sovereign risk pools, but it needs new primary legislation and has no effective date yet.
description:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore wants to give the city-state a legal structure that many insurance centres already offer: the protected cell company. This article was first published in August and has been updated on October 13, 2026 with details from the consultation documents and from reporting on the announcement. According to MAS, the consultation paper, numbered ID 08/26, was issued on July 7, 2026, and comments were due on August 7. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, who chairs MAS, had announced the framework earlier at the Association of Banks in Singapore annual dinner on June 25.

A protected cell company, or PCC, is described in the proposal as a single legal entity made up of a Core and one or more Cells. The Core handles governance and oversight, and the Cells carry on the insurance business. Neither the Core nor a Cell has a separate legal personality, and transactions are carried out through the PCC. The key feature is segregation: each Cell's assets and liabilities are legally separated from the Core and from other Cells. The Core's assets cannot be used to pay a Cell's liabilities, and one Cell's assets cannot be used to meet another Cell's liabilities. Creditors can only claim against the assets of the Core or Cell they dealt with, and contracts must disclose the PCC structure and which Cell is acting. If a Cell fails, it can be wound up as though it were a separate legal person without bringing down the rest of the company.

Why does that matter? MAS says that today a sponsor generally needs a separate legal entity, such as a special purpose vehicle, for each programme. According to Insurance Business, MAS argues that the cost and effort of doing so can deter use. A PCC would let several programmes share one platform, with each one ring-fenced. The initial uses would be captive insurance, including rent-a-captive arrangements in which a sponsor provides a platform for others, insurance-linked securities such as catastrophe bonds, and sovereign risk pools. Singapore's deputy prime minister said PCCs can make captive solutions more accessible for corporates and make it cheaper and faster for sponsors of insurance-linked securities to move risk to the capital markets, complementing traditional reinsurance.

The market backdrop is specific. Singapore is already Asia's largest captive domicile by count, with close to 90 captive insurers according to the Singapore Captive Insurance Association, but it has no cell structure. Labuan, the Malaysian offshore centre, says it is the only Asian jurisdiction offering a PCC, and reported that its captive premiums rose 7.2% to US$726 million in 2025. On the capital-markets side, 29 catastrophe bonds worth more than US$4 billion were issued in Singapore between December 2018 and November 2025, and MAS has extended a grant scheme that offsets part of the upfront cost of issuance to the end of 2028. MAS also cited an estimate that natural disasters caused about US$65 billion of losses in Asia in 2025, with more than 90% uninsured, based on Swiss Re Institute data, and Swiss Re's estimate that the global natural catastrophe protection gap was US$424 billion in 2025, up from US$395 billion.

The legal detail from law-firm analysis gives a sense of how the framework would work in practice. A PCC could issue shares or debentures for the Core or for a Cell, but circular shareholding between Cells and the Core would be banned. Capital reductions, buybacks and conditional dividends are allowed. An existing Singapore company limited by shares could convert into a PCC by special resolution after notifying creditors and making a directors' declaration that no creditor will be materially prejudiced. A PCC could also convert back. Governance would follow the Companies Act, including a minimum number of directors and at least one Singapore-resident director, and the company name would need to include the words "PCC" or "Protected Cell Company." Annual audits would present separate financial information for the Core and each Cell. For tax purposes the PCC would be treated as one entity, goods and services tax would apply at Cell level and each Cell would be a separate person for stamp duty. Existing anti-money-laundering rules for licensed insurers would apply.

The proposal is not law yet. MAS proposes new primary legislation, which is a longer route than a supervisory notice, and the July consultation was the first of two phases. A later consultation will cover the draft PCC Act and subsidiary legislation. MAS has not announced an effective date, and the consultation results have not been published in the sources reviewed. Anyone planning a structure should treat the proposals as subject to change.

Will it work? Aon's regional captive director George Ong said the framework could broaden access to risk financing without the burden of a standalone legal entity and compared it to Singapore's Variable Capital Company structure for funds, which has been used widely by asset managers. Likely users include small and mid-sized companies, larger firms testing a captive before forming an insurance subsidiary, and sponsors of insurance-linked securities. A note of caution came from MAS executive director Lim Cheng Khai, who said at a July 2 captive forum that Asian parents own only 5% to 6% of global captives, and from Swiss Re's estimate that emerging Asia's insurance resilience is about 5%. Insurance Business argued that affordability, awareness and thin local risk capital are demand-side problems that a corporate structure alone will not solve.

For businesses, the practical takeaways are modest for now. Companies thinking about a captive should follow the second consultation and speak to brokers and captive managers about how a cell structure would compare with existing options. For ordinary insurance buyers, the benefits are indirect: more risk capital in the region could, over time, improve the availability of cover for disasters, but that outcome depends on legislation and market take-up.

key_points: MAS issued consultation paper ID 08/26 on July 7, 2026, with comments due on August 7; Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong had announced the plan on June 25.
A protected cell company is one legal entity with a Core and one or more Cells whose assets and liabilities are legally ring-fenced from each other.
Initial uses would be captive insurance, insurance-linked securities and sovereign risk pools, without a new special purpose vehicle for each programme.
Singapore has close to 90 captive insurers and 29 catastrophe bonds worth over US$4 billion issued from December 2018 to November 2025, but no cell structure today.
MAS proposes new primary legislation, a second consultation will cover the draft PCC Act, and no effective date has been announced.
why_it_matters: Companies and governments across Asia are exposed to natural disasters, and most of those losses go uninsured. A cheaper, faster way to set up captives and cat bonds could widen the capital available for risk in the region and strengthen Singapore as a hub, but only if the law passes and the market actually uses it.
